title: Return of the Australian Trio
summary: Amelia Besseny, Cooper Bowman and Yuta Matsumura revisit the group’s earlier records and discuss their free-form approach, trip-hop atmosphere and changing creative chemistry.
transcript:
Amelia Besseny, Cooper Bowman and Yuta Matsumura of Th Blisks joined Lauren Taylor and Simon Winkler in the Triple R studios, ahead of their show at Miscellania for Efficient Space's 10th anniversary. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 29 January 2026. Edited for length and clarity.

Lauren: We're joined in the studio by all three members of the trio, Th Blisks. Is this the first time you've all been in a radio studio together? I can imagine it would be.

Cooper: Yeah. We're spread out across Australia.

Simon: We've got Cooper Bowman, Amelia Besseny and Yuta Matsumura joining us. Thanks so much for being here ahead of your show tomorrow night at Miscellania, celebrating 10 years of the incredible Efficient Space label. Listeners to RRR would be very familiar with all of your projects, individually and collectively: you're so prolific and accomplished across music, academia and other disciplines. Yuta, your bands like Low Life and Oily Boys, and your work with Keanu Nelson, of course: absolute legends. Cooper, running Altered States Tapes, now out of Hobart, a label that started back in 2010 and is now past its 100th release. Amelia, an incredible academic and music maker, classically trained. Cooper and Amelia making music together as Troth. But at some point, Yuta, apparently you invited all three of you to make something a little different as Th Blisks. Is that right?

Yuta: Yeah, that's right.

Simon: What was the catalyst? What made you think, 'I think we can do something together'?

Yuta: At the time, Cooper and I were hanging out with each other a lot. I was going up to Newcastle, I think it was back in 2019 or something. And after a few long nights of talking about music, it just felt right to ask him and Amelia to have a jam together and make some weirdo, whatever you'd call it, trip-hop. I don't like to call it trip-hop, but at the time I was playing around with slowing down jungle beats, and I thought I might test that and see what Cooper can do and Amelia can do as well.

Lauren: So there wasn't a clear concept?

Yuta: No, it wasn't a clear decision. The first recording we did, we did like three songs in a day off that first record, pretty much. You guys came over, I think.

Cooper: Yeah, we came right to yours.

Lauren: What was that first day like?

Cooper: We were hung over. I think those three songs were 'Garfitti', 'Taipei Dubble', all the slow ones. Gives a sense of where we were at.

Lauren: You were soundtracking the mood.

Cooper: Yeah. So we evolved organically after that, and then we did that album pretty quickly. We didn't have any expectations when we went to play the songs, and then we ended up recording a few. It was like, cool, we can do it together. So yeah, it was nice.

Simon: How do you see Th Blisks in relation to your other projects: Yuta, your solo work, and Cooper and Amelia, your work with Troth?

Cooper: I guess it's kind of hard. Sometimes the lines get blurred, because Amelia has a pretty distinctive voice, and those same interests come out in what you're doing. But you try and keep the things distinct. And it's always going to be different with three people involved. It's more of a conversation. So you just try and keep that element, that vitality to it. What do you reckon, Yuta?

Yuta: Yeah, I think that's right. Obviously there are similarities across all three of our projects, but when we're all together making something, it stands out. It's unique compared to — I don't know. I think what we do individually is unique as well. But to me, it's all different.

Cooper: Yeah, and you've got to keep it different. There's more chaos, I guess. Yuta and I especially have pretty different perspectives on things, which comes out, in a way, in what you do.

Lauren: And that's a good thing, though, right?

Cooper: It's different chemistries across different projects, so naturally you're going to get different sounds.

Lauren: You were laughing about those differences of opinion. Is there an example?

Cooper: Oh, you want some drama?

Yuta: Well, I think the way we approach writing music is a lot different. Maybe I'm a bit more chaotic in that sense, a bit more free, but also particular. And I think Cooper — I don't know, you can talk for yourself.

Cooper: No, no, no, go on, go on.

Yuta: I think what you do is you pull samples from a library, and that's a very kind of librarian mentality. When I go into a library, I just go, 'Oh, what's this like? I'm just going to chuck this together.'

Cooper: Yeah. Maybe it's a bit more considered, and that can be a limitation or it can be a strength.

Yuta: I think it's both. And same for me, there are weaknesses. So we hopefully meet in the middle. Amelia's approach is also quite fluid. And I think it's quite ethereal on top of this chaos that Cooper and I have. So it binds really nicely.

Simon: You're playing at Miscellania this Friday, chapter one of Efficient Space's 10th anniversary series, and it's a chance to revisit How So?, the debut of Th Blisks, the album that came out of that momentous first day. How does it feel to see it have a second chapter now on Efficient Space? Maybe, Amelia, how does it feel?

Amelia: Well, I think it's great. And luckily the records came just in time for the show as well, which is always nice. It's a Blisks miracle.

Cooper: It is. When we've played shows as Troth, we've actually had people come up to us overseas, pointing at pictures on their phone, being like, 'This record, make this one again.' And we're like, 'Oh, we'll have to talk to you about that.'

Simon: Because there were 150 copies, and that was it. Is that right?

Cooper: Yeah. Initially. On Altered States originally.

Simon: Has your relationship to the tracks changed over time? Do you hear anything in them now that you perhaps didn't at the time? Maybe for yourself, Cooper?

Cooper: Well, we jammed last week. Yuta came down to Hobart, and we played through the songs properly, for some of them kind of the first time. So you're hearing them in a completely different light. And I think it was kind of exciting to play them, because they take on a new life.

And I hope they're on the right side of looseness. Hopefully that spirit is in them. So it changes over time. If you're playing them for the first time years later, it's kind of an exciting experience more than anything, which is really nice. But just hearing them again, I'm proud of that record. I think it still stands up a few years later.

Yuta: It felt great to play some of the songs together live.

Lauren: We're looking forward to experiencing that magic of you three together tomorrow. Your most recent album, Elixa, was made across three very different locations: Cooper and Amelia, you were in Newcastle and then Hobart, and Yuta, you were out in Papunya for a couple of years. You've described that process as a call and response, rather than the immediacy of being in a room together. What were you actually sending back and forth to each other?

Cooper: You'd have just been like, 'Nah, that's wrong.' That's what you were saying.

Yuta: No, you guys gang up on me: 'Amelia and I don't reckon this is good.' And I'm like, 'I want to hear Amelia say that.' Amelia's too nice.

Cooper: Just a lot of emails. It's hard, because you don't have the immediacy of conversation: if you were together, you'd probably figure it out quicker, so it takes longer. And I think we'd made the pictures for the album before anything, maybe, too. I don't know.

Amelia: Yeah, maybe. So there was a kind of visual language. The rock faces.

Yuta: Oh, no, this is for Elixa, the one we did by correspondence.

Amelia: Oh, yes. That was Oscar's.

Yuta: Yeah, shout out to Oscar for the cover of that. It's a good cover. I feel like that encapsulates what we're doing, though. It's kind of cartoonish, in a sense.

Simon: The melodica is such a distinctive voice on these records. The press release calls it 'fog-thick'. What draws you to that instrument?

Yuta: It's easy to honk. It sounds good when you put it through effects, like Augustus Pablo. I don't know, it just made sense.

Cooper: It's cheap. I mean, a lot of people use it.

Yuta: It's big in Japan.

Cooper: It's huge in Japan.

Amelia: Our cat hates it.

Cooper: When we were jamming, Yuta and I were both playing the melodica because he was trying to teach me a part for one of the songs. Our cat was having a tantrum, screaming at us. Not vibing the frequencies.

Amelia: She's all right with the clarinet.

Lauren: You're sharing the stage with Hydroplane at Miscellania. A Pitchfork review compared Elixa to Hydroplane, in sound and philosophy. What did you think of that comparison? Are they a band you feel aligned with?

Cooper: I mean, I like them. I've always been a fan, like all of us have, of the DIY history of Australia, so it's nice to be somewhere in that lineage. So I guess that does make sense.

Yuta: And, like you said, sort of playfulness. I pick that up in their work. It's experimental, and there's a sense of play in it. That's the stuff of theirs I like the most, the more fringe-dwelling.

Lauren: This is part of a series celebrating 10 years of Efficient Space. You're close friends and collaborators, and having run your own label, you might understand better than most what a milestone that is. Can you tell us about your connection with Efficient Space and how you see their impact?

Cooper: It's one of my favourite labels anywhere operating. So, again, nice to be included in that mix. I respect the scope, but also the focus of what Michael does with it. There's a lot of variation, but there's a consistency. It's all top-shelf stuff. I mean, not trying to big us up. It's nice to be included amongst it, though, is what I'm saying, I guess. And obviously, you go and play in Europe and people are just really supportive and passionate about that label over there. So that sort of speaks volumes about it.

Simon: Amelia, you were talking about how fun it's been to revisit these songs in rehearsals. Is there more Th Blisks material on the horizon? Are you writing as you rehearse the older songs?

Amelia: We've been trying to learn the songs in a very short time frame. Hopefully. There are definitely ideas.

Simon: Yuta, you've been working with Keanu Nelson. How's the album developing? Are there any updates you're in a position to share?

Yuta: Yeah. So I went up to Alice Springs to meet Keanu and Brendan, who usually comes with Keanu whenever we go touring. We met up at his house, so we set up a little studio in Brendan's house and recorded for a week. Within that week we got about 11 tracks. Just kind of smashed it out. So now I'm at a stage where I'm just refining them and mixing those recordings. It's maybe a little bit less sentimental than the first one, and a bit more fun, I guess.

Simon: Thanks so much for joining us.
